messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor is a 73-year-old widow who has made her living for years as a painter, working alone in a converted room at the back of her house. Two years ago, she was caught in a man-made disaster when an intoxicated man forced his way into a small downtown gallery during an evening artists’ reception where several of her paintings were hanging. He shoved past guests, grabbed at people, and overturned bottles and glasses as he moved through the room. Eleanor remembers being knocked down beside a display wall, pinned awkwardly on one hip with her arm trapped under her, unable at first to get up while people screamed and cried around her. What stayed with her most vividly was the smell of spilled alcohol on his breath and clothes, the feel of strangers’ hands pulling at her to move, and the sound of sobbing in the room as everyone tried to understand whether more danger was coming.

Since then, those same cues have become charged in ways that feel immediate rather than symbolic. If someone reaches out and touches her unexpectedly, she stiffens and her body reacts before she can think. If she catches the smell of alcohol on a customer, a neighbor, or even drifting from the street outside her studio, she becomes sharply keyed up, scanning and listening as though someone may be about to come through the door. The sound of crying, even on television or from another room, affects her in much the same way. In those moments she grows irritable and short with people, and at night she lies awake listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering her home.

The triggers do not stay in the present for long. The smell of alcohol or the pressure of a hand on her arm can bring back the gallery with a brutal clarity, “like photographs,” as she describes it, fixed images rather than a story: the tipped glasses, the floor at eye level, shoes moving past her face. When these memories come, her body curls into the same cramped position she had been in that night, as if she is back on the floor with her arm pinned. Crying is especially potent; hearing it can pull up the scene so quickly that she feels she is dropped into it without warning.

Over time Eleanor has come to believe that the disaster broke something permanent in her. She says her old assumptions about people and ordinary safety are gone, that the world no longer works in any reliable way. She has also begun to fear that she will never feel normal emotion again, only agitation, numbness, or guilt. That belief leaves her exquisitely sensitive to the very cues she dreads. She notices tears in a face immediately, the brush of contact in a crowded place, the faintest trace of alcohol, already bracing because she is certain these moments mean she is about to lose control of herself again. The same convictions shape how she remembers the event: whenever the images return, they are saturated with guilt that she survived, that she froze, that others in the room were more frightened or more hurt than she was. Each recollection seems to confirm her sense that her life has narrowed into something damaged and barely worth living.

The memories themselves deepen that conviction. Because they arrive as stark, frozen pictures with the shame and bodily helplessness intact, they do not feel like something finished. After an episode, Eleanor is left thinking not only that the world is unsafe, but that she herself has been permanently altered by what happened. She finds herself saying that she is no longer the woman she was, and in her bleakest moments she is not sure life is worth much now. Once she has been pulled into those images, the ordinary world feels contaminated by reminders; touch becomes harder to tolerate, crying harder to hear, and the smell of alcohol nearly unbearable.

Her days have gradually organized around trying not to set any of this off. She no longer watches the news if there is any chance of coverage of public violence or disasters like the one at the gallery. In her studio she keeps the radio off and works constantly, telling herself that if she can keep her mind occupied mixing paint, stretching canvas, cleaning brushes, then the images will stay down. When they press in anyway, she tries hard not to think about them, sometimes painting late into the night out of sheer mental exhaustion. The cost has been visible. She avoids exhibition openings and declines visitors to her workspace because she cannot tolerate accidental touch or the possibility that someone may arrive smelling of wine. Customers have found her abrupt, and she knows she has become harsher and more easily angered than she ever was before.

At night, after forcing the day into busyness, she often sleeps poorly, listening for sounds at the doors and windows. The vigilance leaves her frayed, and being so on edge seems only to harden her belief that she is beyond repair. What finally brought Eleanor to treatment was a recent incident when a fellow artist embraced her after a local show and she jerked away, smelled wine on the woman’s breath, and spent the rest of the evening shaken, angry, and flooded with images of the gallery floor. She came in frightened that this is how the rest of her life will be—guarded, sleepless, emotionally deadened—and hoping, though only faintly, that the memories might stop feeling as if they are happening all over again.
